title: Why he ignored blues records and prefers ballads
summary: Waters admits skipping Bessie Smith and Ida Cox records because he wanted to be progressive, says he prefers ballads, and explains that too many chords spoil the blues.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: How about Bessie Smith, did you listen to her records?
No, I don't remember listening to Bessie Smith at that period, records, you know.

I'm ashamed of myself now, see, this is gonna (PS laughs), this is gonna be, I'm ashamed of myself. I didn't, wasn't interested that much in blues of that type, you know what I mean? Which I'm ashamed of myself because I should have, you know. Now even now if you've noticed, even now - I'm 80 years old, I played more blues for you in this place [West End] within the last 3 nights, 2 nights, than I ever played since I've been coming here in the last 5 years, 4 years, if you - although you haven't been there every night, but I have. And nothin' wrong with it, I should play more blues, it's obvious. I can play blues, because we had a big success with the last 2, 3 nights playin' blues. But I - you know, this is a personal opinion, see, I'm not sayin' that right - I prefer to play ballads, and pretty ballads. "Laura", "Body And Soul" and pretty songs, that's my kick, that's what I like, that's what I'm happy. But it's nothing wrong with blues. So I find out that the blues are going over very big, so if I come back next year I have to have a more of a elaborated blues repertoire, see? (laughs).

You're shying away from Bessie Smith's records or maybe blues sounds in the middle '20's. Was that sort of an extension of perhaps your opinion that that was a simpler form of music and you were trying -
to be a progressive type of musician?

Yeah, yeah, exactly. Now you can tell - I mean I kinda had proof of that. I tell you why now, wait a minute, I tell you why, I'm glad you brought that up. You remember I told you I's kind of mad about that deal too, when you was tellin' me, when I saw that 80 years old out there with nothing else - remember I told you? I said I don't play like some of the first New Orleans musicians my age, I play more modern, and you said yes, right? Well, that's it, that's the whole thing. Because otherwise I would be playing the same way now as I did in 1920 something, or like, say, I made on that record, on Charlie Johnson - I'd be playin' the same way, exactly. But I'm not. I know that because I have the records of 1926 and I have the records I made last year in England, see what I'm talking about? So that, so I was on that dance kick from the beginning. And that means that - listen, I'm not sayin' I'm right, though, see - but that means that I wasn't listening to something that wasn't more progressive, you see what I mean? I was listening to other things, more advanced. At first when I came to New York even, it was tenor players playin' other than Coleman Hawkins, 'cause a lot of the guys were playin' the blues only and didn't know one chord from the other. We still don't have, in that period - even now - you don't have to know too many chords and be so progressive to play the blues. To tell the truth, if you're too progressive you can't play the blues, you don't sound like the blues, it's too, too high-class, too, you know - you lose that real blues effect if you play too many beautiful chords and things. Blues has got to be simple as it possibly, even in the, naturally we have more progressive now than then, but still, you still it - even Charlie Parker when, he was one of the most progressive, Charlie eliminated many notes, the going to, you've heard that on your record, you play Charlie all the time. You've heard him, when he goes into those long notes, that's what he's doing, he's gettin' a bluesy thing. If he didn't do that, he wouldn't be, he wouldn't have a blues effect. So that's the whole thing, I was more advanced. If I wasn't more advanced then I would be playing the same as some of the guys up there, and most likely I wouldn't be working for you (laughs). With all these young guys like you got around here (laughs), you don't need players - if I couldn't play you wouldn't have me, I wouldn't be workin' nine countries a year for 10 years and makin' money, you know what I mean? That's obvious, because I mean over in France these guys can play, too, you know, in Europe. See what I mean, they play all over world now, not only, so I couldn't afford to be doing, see.
